headline: KSE-100 rockets 1.66% to reclaim 180,000 as Wall Street's Dow hits a record and oil extends its Hormuz-driven slide toward $75
mood: Constructive · oil's slide is the swing factor

five_things.html: The KSE-100 surged 1.66% (+2,931.71 pts) to close at 180,014.93, reclaiming the 180,000 level as breadth turned firmly positive (303 advancers vs 158 decliners) on 740.6m shares (Rs35.9bn) — commercial banks, fertiliser, cement and E&P led, with foreign investors net buyers of Rs771.9m (Express Tribune, Business Recorder).

The Dow rose 0.5% to a record 54,349 for a fifth straight record close, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.17% to 7,723.55 and the Nasdaq fell 0.83% to 26,363.44, snapping a four-day rally as investors rotated out of megacap tech (CNBC, TheStreet).

Brent fell 0.3% to $79.15 and WTI slid 0.7% toward $75 as Iran reportedly reached an agreement with Oman on a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, deepening a two-day, 10%+ drawdown on reopening hopes (Rigzone, Trading Economics).

Gold held near $4,096 (+0.44%) while silver punched to $62.50, its highest since June, even as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish 29 July hold keeps September rate-hike odds elevated near 61% — down from over 82% pre-meeting but still hawkish-leaning (Yahoo Finance, Yahoo Finance).

Saudi's non-oil PMI held at 53.1 in July while the UAE's jumped to 52.7 from 50.8 — new export orders grew for the first time since March — as Gulf economies rebound from wartime lows, even as Section 301 forced-labor tariff exposure (10–12.5%) lingers over both markets (AGBI, Semafor).

matrix.local_html: Wednesday's session saw the KSE-100 surge 1.66% to 180,014.93, adding 2,931.71 points to reclaim the 180,000 level after slipping to an intraday low of 178,512.09 in early trade. Breadth turned firmly positive — 303 advancers against 158 decliners (35 unchanged) on 740.6 million shares (Rs35.9bn) — while foreign investors were net buyers to the tune of Rs771.9m. Commercial banks, fertiliser, cement, exploration & production, oil marketing companies, power generation, investment companies and technology stocks led the advance, with HBL, UBL, Meezan Bank, Engro Holdings, Fauji Fertiliser, MCB, Lucky Cement, Systems Ltd and Hub Power among the top performers. The rally was underpinned by easing US-Iran tensions, Brent's slide from the mid-$80s toward $78, and reports that Islamabad is seeking Chinese refinancing of a $1.3bn commercial loan. On the macro front, headline CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting on 27 July. Six-month KIBOR is tracking near 11.70–11.90% (EST.), broadly in line with the policy rate. The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/second RSF review on 8 May, unlocking roughly $1.1bn (EFF) and $220m (RSF); the next review is expected in H2 2026.
matrix.gcc_html: Gulf non-oil momentum held up in July: Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI stayed at a robust 53.1 (53.3 in June) on firmer domestic demand, even as export orders fell for a fifth straight month on elevated freight costs. The UAE's non-oil PMI jumped to 52.7 from 50.8, with new orders at a five-month high and export orders growing for the first time since March, as Gulf economies dig out from wartime lows. Oil kept sliding on the diplomatic thaw: Brent fell to $79.15 and WTI slid toward $75 after Iran reportedly reached an agreement with Oman on a Strait of Hormuz shipping route — a bearish setup for crude that nonetheless keeps the Gulf's non-oil diversification story (Vision 2030, PIF-backed giga-projects) intact. Washington's Section 301 forced-labor tariff investigation, covering roughly 60 economies including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, remains a live overhang on Gulf exporters even as new corporate-transparency rules bed in.
matrix.global_html: Wall Street closed mixed on Wednesday: the Dow added 263 points (+0.5%) to a record 54,349, its fifth straight record close, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.17% to 7,723.55 and the Nasdaq fell 0.83% to 26,363.44, snapping a four-day rally as a tech rotation offset broader gains. Bonds stayed cautious: the 10-year yield sits near 4.63% and the 2-year at 4.21%, with markets pricing September rate-hike odds near 61% — down from over 82% before the July FOMC but still elevated — after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish-tinted 29 July hold left his inflation-fighting credibility under scrutiny. Washington's trade agenda keeps moving: a 50% tariff on Canadian goods takes effect 19 August — now five days out — while Pakistan's own reciprocal tariff with the US sits at a comparatively favourable 19% (down from a proposed 29%), and Section 301 forced-labor duties of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies remain in force since 24 July.

legislative.policy_html: Finance Act 2026's 5% withholding tax (10% for non-filers) on digital creators' social media earnings remains in force, with banks deducting it at source since 30 July; separately, reports emerged that Islamabad is seeking Chinese refinancing of a $1.3bn commercial loan.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: FBR compliance-tech vendors, formal-sector filers, and near-term external-financing relief if the Chinese rollover proceeds. Loses: non-filer creators facing the 10% deduction; the refinancing request underscores continued external-liquidity strain.

legislative.policy_html: Washington's Section 301 forced-labor investigation keeps Saudi Arabia and the UAE among roughly 60 economies facing 10–12.5% duties on flagged goods, even as Saudi's new Companies Law and the UAE's Cabinet Decision 59/2026 tighten corporate transparency and beneficial-ownership disclosure.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: compliant multinationals and institutional investors gaining disclosure. Loses: Gulf exporters absorbing forced-labor tariff exposure; SMEs facing new registry and compliance overhead.

legislative.policy_html: The 50% US tariff on Canadian goods takes effect 19 August — now five days out — while Pakistan's negotiated 19% reciprocal tariff (down from a proposed 29%) with Washington remains in force.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: Pakistani textile and apparel exporters gaining a relative tariff advantage over higher-taxed peers. Loses: Canadian exporters and US importers/retailers facing the 19 August step-up in duties.

levels.support_note: Wednesday's intraday low; deeper support at 177,100 (Tuesday's close)
levels.resistance_note: Wednesday's intraday high; then the psychological 182,000 level

desk_stance_html: Desk view: Wednesday's 1.66% surge reclaimed 180,000 on broad, breadth-confirmed buying (303 advancers vs 158 decliners) with foreign investors net buyers (Rs771.9m) — a healthier setup than last week's institutional profit-taking. Falling oil is the key tailwind: Brent's slide toward $79 and WTI toward $75 on Hormuz de-escalation hopes eases Pakistan's import bill and inflation outlook, reinforcing the case for the SBP's rate hold. Sector leadership in banks, fertiliser and cement suggests rotation into value rather than pure momentum-chasing. Watch 178,500 as the first floor; a close below re-opens 177,100. On the upside, clearing Wednesday's 180,202 high opens the psychological 182,000 mark. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.

🌅 Economic Vibes — Morning Brief | Thursday, 06 August 2026

The KSE-100 stormed back above 180,000 while Wall Street closed mixed at fresh records — here's what the desk is watching this morning.

THE OVERNIGHT TAPE
Dow +0.5% to a record 54,349 (fifth straight record close), while the S&P 500 slipped 0.17% to 7,723.55 and the Nasdaq fell 0.83% to 26,363.44, snapping a four-day tech rally as investors rotated out of megacap growth. US 10Y sits at 4.63%, 2Y at 4.21%, with September rate-hike odds easing to ~61% (from over 82% pre-FOMC) after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish 29 July hold.

PAKISTAN
KSE-100 surged 1.66% to close at 180,014.93 (+2,931.71 pts), reclaiming the 180,000 level on broad, breadth-confirmed buying — 303 advancers vs 158 decliners on 740.6m shares (Rs35.9bn) — led by banks, fertiliser, cement and E&P. Foreign investors were net buyers (Rs771.9m). Reports emerged that Islamabad is seeking Chinese refinancing of a $1.3bn commercial loan. On the macro side: CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July, and the SBP held its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting; six-month KIBOR tracks near 11.70–11.90% (desk est.).

GCC
Saudi's non-oil PMI held at a robust 53.1 in July; the UAE's jumped to 52.7 from 50.8 as new export orders grew for the first time since March — Gulf economies rebounding from wartime lows. Oil kept sliding: Brent fell to $79.15, WTI toward $75, as Iran reportedly reached an agreement with Oman on a Hormuz shipping route, deepening a two-day 10%+ drawdown.

GLOBAL
Gold is holding near $4,096 (+0.44%), and silver popped to $62.50 — its highest since June — as havens stayed bid despite record US equities. Washington's trade agenda keeps moving: the 50% tariff on Canadian goods lands in five days (19 August), and Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10–12.5% on ~60 economies, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE) remain in force; Pakistan's own reciprocal tariff with the US sits at a comparatively favourable 19%.

LEGISLATIVE TRACKER
Pakistan's Finance Act 2026 digital-creator withholding tax (5%/10%) continues to be deducted at source by banks.
Section 301 forced-labor duties keep Saudi/UAE exporters exposed even as new corporate-transparency rules (Saudi Companies Law, UAE Cabinet Decision 59/2026) tighten disclosure.
The Canada tariff step-up (19 August) and Pakistan's 19% US tariff rate reshape relative trade competitiveness across textiles and manufacturing.

THE DAY AHEAD
KSE-100: support 178,500 (Wednesday's intraday low, deeper at 177,100), pivot 180,015 (Wednesday's close), resistance 180,200 (Wednesday's high, then the psychological 182,000).
Desk view: breadth-confirmed buying and foreign inflows argue for a healthier tape than last week's profit-taking; falling oil remains the key tailwind for Pakistan's import bill. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.
